questions.question: What is a Promise in JavaScript? Explain its states and lifecycle.
questions.title: JavaScript Promise Lifecycle — States, then, catch, finally
questions.direct_answer:
What is a Promise in JavaScript? Explain its states and lifecycle.

**In one line:** name the mechanism, where it applies (the type checker, emit pipeline, and how types line up with runtime JS), and the user-visible outcome.

**Interviewers dig into:** Three states (pending, fulfilled, rejected); immutability after settling; then/catch/finally chaining; microtask scheduling.

**Classic weak answer:** Saying a Promise can go from fulfilled to rejected — once settled, a Promise's state is immutable.

**Senior finish:** Mention that Promise callbacks run as microtasks (before next macrotask), explain unhandled-rejection behavior, and reference AbortController for cancellation.

interviewer_intent.testing: Three states (pending, fulfilled, rejected); immutability after settling; then/catch/finally chaining; microtask scheduling
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying a Promise can go from fulfilled to rejected — once settled, a Promise's state is immutable
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that Promise callbacks run as microtasks (before next macrotask), explain unhandled-rejection behavior, and reference AbortController for cancellation

sections.title: Why this question matters
sections.content:
This question — **JavaScript Promise Lifecycle — States, then, catch, finally** — shows up constantly in **frontend / fullstack** interviews because it separates candidates who memorized docs from candidates who can **reason about real systems**.

**Restate the prompt:** What is a Promise in JavaScript? Explain its states and lifecycle.

A gold-level answer does four things in order:

1. **Define** the terms in plain English (what it is / what problem it solves).
2. **Explain the mechanism** (what runs when: browser, bundler, framework, network).
3. **Compare trade-offs** (speed vs correctness vs security vs DX) with **when you would not use** the default.
4. **Ground it in production** — caching, auth, observability, tests, or an incident you handled.

Interviewers are listening for: **Three states (pending, fulfilled, rejected); immutability after settling; then/catch/finally chaining; microtask scheduling**.

The fastest way to lose points is: **Saying a Promise can go from fulfilled to rejected — once settled, a Promise's state is immutable**.

If you only add one “senior” layer, make it: **Mention that Promise callbacks run as microtasks (before next macrotask), explain unhandled-rejection behavior, and reference AbortController for cancellation**.

sections.title: Deep dive — what to say
sections.content:
### What to explain (middle of the answer)

- **Core mechanics:** Three states (pending, fulfilled, rejected); immutability after settling; then/catch/finally chaining; microtask scheduling
- **Concrete shape:** give a small code or config snippet *only if it clarifies* (5–15 lines max).
- **Interviewer follow-ups:** expect “what breaks in production?”, “how do you debug?”, “what would you measure?” — answer them proactively.

### How to sound senior (without rambling)

- Tie the feature to **user-visible outcomes** (performance, accessibility, security).
- Mention **one failure mode** you have actually seen (race, stale cache, hydration mismatch, flaky test).
- Close with **one decision rule** (“choose X when …; choose Y when …”).

questions.question: What is the difference between async/await and Promises? When should you use each?
questions.title: async/await vs Promises — Differences, Benefits & When to Use Each
questions.direct_answer:
What is the difference between async/await and Promises? When should you use each?

**In one line:** name the mechanism, where it applies (the type checker, emit pipeline, and how types line up with runtime JS), and the user-visible outcome.

**Interviewers dig into:** async/await is syntactic sugar over promises; it reads synchronously, handles errors with try/catch, and is easier to debug; promises still shine for parallelism and chaining.

**Classic weak answer:** Forgetting async/await is still Promise-based (an async function always returns a Promise), and using `.then()` inside async just to mix styles.

**Senior finish:** Explain when to use Promise.all with async/await for concurrency (don't await sequentially when operations are independent); discuss top-level await.

questions.question: What is the difference between Promise.all, Promise.allSettled, Promise.race, and Promise.any?
questions.title: Promise.all vs allSettled vs race vs any — When to Use Each
questions.direct_answer:
What is the difference between Promise.all, Promise.allSettled, Promise.race, and Promise.any?

**In one line:** name the mechanism, where it applies (the type checker, emit pipeline, and how types line up with runtime JS), and the user-visible outcome.

**Interviewers dig into:** all rejects fast on any failure; allSettled waits for all outcomes; race settles with the first to settle; any resolves with the first fulfilled (AggregateError on all-rejected).

**Classic weak answer:** Using Promise.all when any request may legitimately fail — a single reject discards all results; allSettled is the right choice.

**Senior finish:** Map each to a real-world use case: all for dependent fan-out, allSettled for dashboards, race for timeouts, any for fastest-of-N mirrors.

interviewer_intent.testing: all rejects fast on any failure; allSettled waits for all outcomes; race settles with the first to settle; any resolves with the first fulfilled (AggregateError on all-rejected)

sections.title: Why this question matters
sections.content:
This question — **Error Handling in async/await — try/catch, Promise.catch & Patterns** — shows up constantly in **frontend / fullstack** interviews because it separates candidates who memorized docs from candidates who can **reason about real systems**.

**Restate the prompt:** How do you handle errors in async/await? What are the best practices?

A gold-level answer does four things in order:

1. **Define** the terms in plain English (what it is / what problem it solves).
2. **Explain the mechanism** (what runs when: browser, bundler, framework, network).
3. **Compare trade-offs** (speed vs correctness vs security vs DX) with **when you would not use** the default.
4. **Ground it in production** — caching, auth, observability, tests, or an incident you handled.

Interviewers are listening for: **try/catch for awaited calls, .catch on the returned promise, centralized error wrappers, and handling unhandled rejections globally**.

The fastest way to lose points is: **Forgetting to await an async function — the returned promise's rejection escapes try/catch and becomes an unhandled rejection**.

If you only add one “senior” layer, make it: **Show Go-style [err, data] = await to() wrappers; mention window.addEventListener('unhandledrejection') and process.on('unhandledRejection') in Node**.

sections.title: Deep dive — what to say
sections.content:
### What to explain (middle of the answer)

- **Core mechanics:** try/catch for awaited calls, .catch on the returned promise, centralized error wrappers, and handling unhandled rejections globally
- **Concrete shape:** give a small code or config snippet *only if it clarifies* (5–15 lines max).
- **Interviewer follow-ups:** expect “what breaks in production?”, “how do you debug?”, “what would you measure?” — answer them proactively.

### How to sound senior (without rambling)

- Tie the feature to **user-visible outcomes** (performance, accessibility, security).
- Mention **one failure mode** you have actually seen (race, stale cache, hydration mismatch, flaky test).
- Close with **one decision rule** (“choose X when …; choose Y when …”).

sections.title: Trade-offs & senior signal
sections.content:
### Trade-offs interviewers expect you to name

- **Speed vs safety** (types, runtime checks, validation).
- **DX vs constraints** (framework magic vs explicit wiring).
- **SEO / first paint vs interactivity** (SSR/SSG/CSR choices where relevant).
- **Security vs convenience** (tokens, cookies, localStorage, third-party scripts).

### What “book answer” misses

- **Book answer:** repeats definitions.
- **Strong answer:** names **forgetting to await an async function — the returned promise's rejection escapes try/catch and becomes an unhandled rejection** and what you do instead.
